extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTAB attorneys, and IP litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and practitioner-focused analysis of PTAB precedential and informative decisions (notably Fintiv and Toshiba) addressing discretionary denial standards, filing-date/payment evidence issues, POP review practice, and related procedural topics. Useful for attorneys litigating petitions (IPR/PGR) and advising on PTAB strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv six-factor test for discretionary denial under §314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The status and anticipated trial date of a related district court or ITC proceeding should weigh into the board’s decision to discretionarily deny an IPR or PGR petition under § 314(a). The six-factor test for application of discretionary denial based on a related proceeding was formalised in Apple v Fintiv (IPR2020-00019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should expect panels to apply the six-factor Fintiv analysis when a parallel proceeding exists; supplemental briefing was authorised in Fintiv to address these factors. Petitioners can respond by using stipulations about prior art/invalidity grounds they will give up in the related proceeding to reduce the weight of a parallel proceeding. Subsequent precedential/informative cases provided guidance on how to apply the six factors in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and weight of stipulations in Fintiv analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners may submit stipulations indicating prior art or invalidity grounds that would be given up in the related proceeding if the IPR were instituted; tribunals compare stipulations of differing breadth when deciding how much weight to afford them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Sotera Wireless v Masimo and Sand Revolution II v Continental Intermodal compared stipulation breadth and illustrated that broader or more specific stipulations are afforded different weights. When drafting stipulations, consider breadth carefully — narrower, precise stipulations may carry different persuasive force than sweeping concessions. Use stipulations strategically to mitigate discretionary denial risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-factor test for discretionary denial under §325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: A six-factor test applies for exercising discretionary denial under § 325(d) when a petition is based on the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments as previously considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test helps panels determine when to deny institution because the petition duplicates prior art/arguments. Expect panels to analyze overlap in grounds and the reasons the petition adds (or fails to add) substantive new argumentation or evidence beyond the earlier proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying real parties in interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions have provided guidance on how to identify real parties in interest for PTAB proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly naming and disclosing real parties in interest is a recurring procedural requirement; failure to identify RPI can affect institution and case management. Follow precedential guidance to determine who must be disclosed based on control, funding, or other relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreements required with a joint motion to terminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance exists on what agreements must be filed with a joint motion to terminate a PTAB proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties move jointly to terminate, the board expects certain agreements to be filed (or appropriate redactions/explanations if confidential). Ensure compliance with the precedential/informative decisions that detail what must accompany a termination motion to avoid denial or delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the board may sua sponte apply new grounds to substitute claims with a motion to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedential/informative decisions discuss when the board may sua sponte apply new grounds of rejection to substitute claims included with a motion to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels consider whether substitute claims introduce new grounds that were not fully litigated and whether the board can raise such grounds sua sponte. Practitioners should craft motions to amend and substitute claims with awareness of these limits to avoid unexpected new-ground rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing-date determination and sufficiency of Fedwire confirmation under 35 U.S.C. §312(a) and 37 C.F.R. §42.103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether Fedwire confirmation of payment constitutes sufficient evidence of payment for establishing a petition filing date was a central question in Toshiba America (IPR2021-00330) and the subject of POP review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels may require evidence that a wire transfer was 'accepted by the Treasury' or that the payment was 'immediate, final and irrevocable.' General descriptions of Fedwire functionality may be insufficient; specific evidence about the petitioner's wire transfer is persuasive. Compliance with USPTO published instructions for wire transfers and proof of initiation on the claimed date can support an earlier filing date. Pre-established deposit accounts with the USPTO can avoid receipt-timing issues tied to wire transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: POP review standards and when POP grants review
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB Precedential Opinion Panel (POP) grants review sparingly and typically when the guiding law or regulation is unclear when applied to a unique fact pattern — e.g., 'Does Fedwire confirmation of payment constitute sufficient evidence of payment under 35 USC § 312(a) and 37 CFR § 42.103(a)?' was deemed to warrant POP review in Toshiba America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POP review is rare (only the fifth grant since 2018 in the cited year) and is used to clarify unsettled legal or regulatory questions. Parties seeking POP review should frame issues as requiring clarification of governing law/regulation across panels. Expect page limits on briefs (the POP authorised initial and responsive 15-page briefs in Toshiba America) and that oral hearings may or may not be scheduled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice: avoid filing at or near the one-year statutory bar date
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing petitions at or near the one-year bar date creates practical risks and may trigger additional expense and time (including POP review) if timing or payment issues arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid unnecessary cost/time, practitioners should file well before the one-year date or maintain pre-established deposit accounts with the USPTO to minimize wire-transfer timing issues. Last-minute filings combined with non-deposit-account wire transfers can produce complex factual disputes about filing dates.
